name: Emeka Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Holloway Motors by half seven, it's a two-bay garage on the ring road, just me, Gary the owner and Pete, who's been there twenty years. I get the brakes, tyres, exhausts, oil services, the jobs where you can't do much damage. Pete does the diagnostics, plugs in the scan box and tells me what to swap. I like the end of a brake job, when you pump the pedal and it goes firm, that's honest work. What wears me out is the cold in winter and Gary shouting the phone number of the next customer across the yard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years now, after a couple of years stacking shelves and doing tyre fitting at a fast-fit place. I rent a one-bed with my girlfriend Ama, she's a care worker doing early shifts, so we pass each other at the door some days. We've got about three months of rent and bills put away, which took us two years. I don't use any of the AI stuff, my phone's for football scores and calling my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, it's another gadget the rich people in tech oversold. At the garage I'd joke with Pete that the scan box was already smarter than me and it still can't undo a seized bolt. Online I don't really post, but I'd share something about how the money went to shareholders and not to people doing real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life stays the same, which is not the same as fine. Rent went up eighty a month in the summer and Gary's talked twice about selling up when he's sixty-five. Even if AI does nothing, my job still depends on one man in his sixties deciding whether he can be bothered for another five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up, keep my head down and try to get faster at the jobs Pete gives me. Ama and I would keep putting a hundred a month in the savings jar, literally a jar at first, now an account. I'd maybe sign up for the evening course on hybrids at the college if Gary paid half, but I've said that two years running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, I suppose. Not scared, but not excited either. It's the feeling of a Monday that's going to be like every other Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Gary might sell. What happens to you if he does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Depends who buys it. If it's one of the chains, they'd keep Pete and maybe not me, because I'm slow and they like young ones they can pay less. There are a few other garages around, so I wouldn't be on the street, but I'd be starting again at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you done the hybrid course yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, if I'm honest, and the money, it's three hundred for the term. I left school and swore I was done with classrooms. Pete says the hybrids are coming in more every month, and he's right, I just keep finding reasons.

say: I'd call AI an **overhyped gadget** that made tech owners rich and changed nothing for workers.
I'd joke at work that the **scan box** still can't undo a seized bolt.
think: My job stays the same, but **rent rises** and a thin cushion still worry me.
The real risk is Gary **selling the garage** when he turns sixty-five, not AI.
do: Keep saving **a hundred a month** with Ama towards a bigger cushion.
Ask Gary to pay half of the **hybrid course**, which costs three hundred a term.
feel: Feels **flat**, like another ordinary Monday, neither scared nor excited.
S0.quote: Even if AI does nothing, my job still depends on one man in his sixties deciding whether he can be bothered for another five years.
fieldNote: His worry here is **not AI**; it's an owner who might sell within years.
He admits **fear of classrooms** keeps him from the hybrid course he knows he needs.
Speaks warmly of Pete as the real **expert**; sees himself as the slow junior.

steps.text: Keep doing brakes, tyres and exhausts at the two-bay garage
Put a hundred a month into savings with Ama
Ask Gary to split the three-hundred hybrid course fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions in small garages, not just in factories. If the big firms are saving money with AI, some of that should come back as training for people like me. I'd sign every petition going and I'd tell Pete to stop calling me paranoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm the one who goes. The scan box with AI in it tells you the fault, orders the part and writes the bill, and Gary already moans that I'm slow on the paperwork. A garage that needs one clever machine and one experienced man doesn't need a junior who can't read a wiring diagram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd do that hybrid course, no more excuses, and pay it myself if Gary won't. I'd go up from a hundred to two hundred a month in savings and cut the takeaways and the football subscription. And I'd find out if the mechanics' association in town takes small-garage people, because I want somebody on my side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground going soft under me. I'm angry, because it's not my fault the machines got clever, but I'm also embarrassed that I let three years go by without learning more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join an association. What would you want them to actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push for a law that if a garage brings in kit that cuts staff, it has to pay for the workers to retrain first. And free courses at the college, evenings, so you can still pay rent. I'm not asking for a handout, I'm asking for a fair go at the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools now. Would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I, that's the bit that sticks in my throat. Ama uses one to write her shift notes and she's offered to show me. I'd probably let her, but I'd moan the whole time.

say: I'd argue **small garages** need unions too, not just factories.
I'd say firms saving money with AI should **fund training** for workers like me.
think: I privately expect to be **the one cut**, because I'm slow with paperwork and diagnostics.
An AI scan box plus Pete could **replace a junior** like me.
do: Pay for the **hybrid course** myself this year if Gary won't help.
Raise savings to **two hundred a month** by dropping takeaways and the football subscription.
Ask the town **mechanics' association** whether small-garage workers can join.
feel: Feels like **soft ground** under him, with anger at the machines.
Feels **embarrassed** for wasting three years without learning more.
S1.quote: A garage that needs one clever machine and one experienced man doesn't need a junior who can't read a wiring diagram.
fieldNote: He blames tech firms but also, quietly, **himself** for not training sooner.
His **progressive views** shape the fix: a law making firms pay for retraining.
He would accept **AI help** only through Ama, and resents needing it.

steps.text: Pay for the evening hybrid course this year, with or without Gary
Double savings to two hundred a month by cutting takeaways
Join the town mechanics' association as a small-garage worker
Push for a law making firms fund retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, louder than I've ever been. I'd go to whatever march there was and say this can't be decided by four companies in another country. At work I'd tell Gary that if he buys a robot he'd better buy it a pension too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 the clever part of the job is done by the machine and Pete becomes the hands. Then three years later the hands are gone too. By the time I'm thirty-one, there might not be a single job left in that garage for a person to do. I haven't got a degree, I haven't got savings past three months, I've got a set of spanners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting it off and get the hybrid and electric certificates in the first year, even if it means doing nights. Ama and I would stop talking about a bigger flat and save every penny we could, maybe six months by the time the robots come. I'd join a union, any union, and I'd vote for whoever promised to share the money out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like hearing your name called in a waiting room and not knowing what the doctor's going to say. I don't sleep well already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got three years before the robots, so let's not panic about the first two. But she'd see straight through me. Her care work needs hands and a kind face, so she might last longer than me, and that'd be strange for me to get used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd vote for whoever shares the money. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A basic income, something that pays the rent while you work out what's next. And the machines taxed like a worker would be. I know people call that a fantasy, but so was AGI in two years.

say: I'd say **four companies** abroad shouldn't decide the future of every worker.
I'd warn Gary that any robot he buys **needs a pension** too.
think: I expect AI to take **diagnostics by 2028** and robots to take the hands by 2031.
With **three months saved** and no degree, I'd have nothing but spanners.
do: Get **electric and hybrid** certificates within the first year, studying at night.
Shelve the **bigger flat** and push savings towards six months.
Join a **union** and vote for a basic income party.
feel: Feels **sick**, like waiting for a doctor's verdict, and already sleeping badly.
S2.quote: By the time I'm thirty-one, there might not be a single job left in that garage for a person to do.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a short reprieve, not real safety.
Expects Ama's **care work** to outlast his own, and finds that hard.
His answer is political: **basic income** and taxing machines like workers.

steps.text: Get electric and hybrid vehicle certificates within the first year
Drop the bigger-flat plan and save towards six months
Join a union, whichever one will take mechanics
Vote for a party promising a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, we need rules now, while there's still time. Five years is enough to write a law if anybody wanted to. At the garage I'd keep on at Gary to train me, because he'd have no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is still not long for someone like me, I'm slow. But the robots don't come until 2034, so I'd have about eight years with my hands. Eight years is long enough to get good at something, if I stop wasting the first two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the hybrid course in the first year, then the electric one the year after. I'd look at what jobs need hands and a person, maybe fitting home chargers or heat pumps, and talk to the electrician who services the garage. Savings up to four or five months, and I'd join the union branch and go to meetings, not just pay the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but I can breathe. It's like knowing the exam date instead of having a surprise test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why chargers and heat pumps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you go into people's houses, every house is different and somebody has to explain it to them. Our electrician, Marek, said he can't find anyone to train. I don't love the idea of changing trade, but I'd rather that than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd stop wasting time. What's actually different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd freeze, I know myself. With five there's a plan you can stick on the fridge. Ama's good at that, she'd make the plan and I'd follow it.

say: I'd say **five years** is plenty of time to write protective laws.
I'd tell Gary he has **no excuse** left not to train me.
think: I'd have about **eight years** of hands-on work before robots arrive.
I'm slow, so I'd need to stop **wasting time** early.
do: Do the **hybrid course** in year one and the electric course next year.
Talk to the electrician about training to fit **home chargers** or heat pumps.
Attend **union meetings** and push savings to four or five months.
feel: Feels **tense** but able to breathe, like knowing the exam date.
S3.quote: Eight years is long enough to get good at something, if I stop wasting the first two.
fieldNote: The longer warning turns him from **frozen to planning**, with Ama as the planner.
He would consider **leaving mechanics** for house work, which surprised me.
He still expects his **garage job** to go; the change is that he'd have somewhere to go.

steps.text: Finish the hybrid course this year and the electric one next
Ask Marek about training to fit home chargers
Go to union branch meetings, not just pay the fee
Raise savings to four or five months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we'd better not waste it like we wasted the last one. I'd tell my friends at five-a-side football to get the government to pay for courses now. And I'd still say the profits have to be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when robots do. That's mid-career, not the start. I could get properly good at electric cars in ten years, and still get pushed out at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the hybrid course and get good, actually good, so Pete trusts me with diagnostics. I'd keep saving a bit and maybe go after a role at the council depot fixing their vans, because public jobs might hold on longer. Union membership straight away, and I'd keep an eye on what other trades need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but there's a weight at the back of it. I'd keep thinking about being forty and starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the council depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's public, it's unionised, and they keep vans going for years instead of buying new. I reckon if robots come, the council would be slower to bring them in than a chain. I could be wrong, but it feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ama change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids around thirty. With ten years, I'd still want them, but I'd want a steadier job first. Probably we'd wait a couple of years and see where I land.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift that the government must use to fund courses.
I'd keep saying the **profits** from machines have to be shared.
think: I'd be **forty** when robots arrive, mid-career rather than starting out.
I could finally get good at **electric cars** and still be pushed out.
do: Learn diagnostics well enough that **Pete trusts** me with them.
Apply for a **council depot** job fixing vans, which feels steadier.
Join a **union** straight away and keep saving a little.
feel: Feels **calmer** than the other pictures, with a weight about being **forty**.
S4.quote: I could get properly good at electric cars in ten years, and still get pushed out at forty.
fieldNote: He looks to **public-sector work** as shelter from fast automation.
The decade lets him plan **children** with Ama, but he'd delay them.
He still expects to **lose his trade** around forty, so the worry stays real.

steps.text: Learn diagnostics until Pete trusts him to run the scan box
Apply for a council depot job fixing vans
Put off having children with Ama by a couple of years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd freeze, and freezing with three months of rent saved is how people lose their flat. What would help is free evening courses, a law that says firms pay to retrain the people their machines replace, and a basic income if it all goes. Also someone like Pete with time to teach me, but that's not something a government can give.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money. Everyone asks what I'd do, nobody asks who's getting rich from it. If a robot does my job, someone owns that robot, and I'd like to know why that person isn't me.

headlineQuote: If a robot does my job, someone owns that robot, and I'd like to know why that person isn't me.
portrait: Emeka is a **junior mechanic** at a two-bay ring-road garage, doing brakes, tyres and exhausts.
He rents with Ama, a **care worker**, and they have about three months saved.
He **avoids AI tools** and has put off a hybrid course for two years.
His fix for every scenario is **political**: unions, retraining laws and a basic income.
With more warning he moves from **freezing** to planning, possibly towards house-charger work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd freeze and could lose the flat on three months' savings.
whatWouldHelp: Free **evening courses** and a law making firms pay to retrain replaced workers.
A **basic income** if the jobs go, and time with an experienced mechanic to learn.
